title: C6F Operation Avalanche
description: 260114-N-PS829-1001 SALERNO, Italy (Jan. 14, 2026) - Vice Adm. Anderson commander of U.S. Naval Sixth Fleet, and LT. Col. Anthony Sama, U.S. Marine Corps, talk about operation avalanche and the battle of Salerno, the significance of the battle and why it is important to work with our allied forces in Salerno, Italy, Jan. 21, 2026. (U.S. Navy video by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Karris Battle)
unit_name: U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Africa/U.S. Sixth Fleet

transcript.text: September 9th , 1943 , under the cover
of darkness , the Allies braced for one
of World War II's most risky missions ,
Operation Avalanche . The goal , a
surprise amphibious landing at Salerno
to pave the way for the liberation of
Italy . The obstacle a reinforced
German army not yet defeated in Sicily ,
anticipating the invasion . Despite a
lack of initial artillery fire , the
Allies consolidated forces over 30
miles of coastline near Salerno and
Pesto . The battle continued for over a
week with the Allies suffering heavy
casualties , but with the support of US
and Royal Navy warships providing naval
gunfire , the Allies blunted the German
counterattack . Minesweeps and air
cover were also essential to enabling
the landing force , which numbered over
150,000 soldiers and about 20,000
vehicles . By September 25th , the
Allies opened the port of Salerno , and
on October 6th , the Allies secured
Naples and all of southern Italy . The
battle was over , but the long road to
Rome and the end of the war was ahead .
Operation Avalanche taught us a brutal
but vital lesson . Victory in Europe
was never guaranteed , and it was not
achieved alone . Just as combined
Allied firepower turned the tide then ,
our strength now lies in a synchronized
effort with our allies and partners .
Deterrence is not a solitary endeavor .
It requires ready , lethal forces
postured to defend our shared interests .
We are and always will be stronger
together .
